newsitem.title: USA: Clinton sends envoys to Mexico on drugs mission.
newsitem.headline: Clinton sends envoys to Mexico on drugs mission.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton sent top White House staff on a surprise visit to Mexico on Wednesday to strengthen anti-drugs ties damaged by the embarrassing arrest of Mexico's top anti-drugs warrior last month.

U.S. drug chief Barry McCaffrey, Acting National Security Advisor Samuel "Sandy" Berger and Clinton's special envoy to Latin America Thomas "Mack" McLarty met with Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo in a clear effort to smoothe troubled waters.

"We have come here today at the request of President Clinton to meet with our colleagues and with President Zedillo to express President Clinton's commitment to strengthening the U.S.-Mexico relationship, based on mutual respect and shared interests, including in our common fight against drugs," Berger told reporters at Zedillo's office.

Mexico's ties with Washington were badly shaken by the arrest of Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, McCaffrey's counterpart in Mexico, in February on charges he was taking pay-offs from the country's top druglord, Amado Carillo Fuentes.

The scandal hit just before Clinton was scheduled to carry out his annual "certification" of foreign countries to assess their cooperation in the war on drugs, and caused an uproar in the U.S. Congress among critics of Mexico's drugs record.
Last Friday, Clinton overrode those critics and renewed certification of Mexico, but he also instructed his government to monitor the country's anti-narcotics efforts closely.

The three American officials, sensitive to the passions it has whipped up in Mexico, made no mention of the certification process or of Gutierrez's arrest. They also refused to take questions. A Mexican government source said they were leaving Mexico the same day.

Another reason for their trip, Mexican officials said, was to tie up loose ends ahead of Clinton's first state visit to Mexico on April 11-12. Controversy over Mexico's commitment to combatting drugs has threatened to cloud the visit.

Clinton's decision to approve Mexico as an ally in the war on drugs failed to mollify many Mexicans, who smarted visibly over having their anti-drug credentials criticised in public in the United States, a country they note is the world's biggest drug consumer.

Opposition legislators have also expressed concerns about reports in the U.S. press that Zedillo's government agreed to a set of U.S. conditions in order to win certification, including giving U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration agents the right to carry arms in Mexico.
Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria denied to legislators at a briefing on Tuesday that any conditions were put on certification. In Congress, left-wing deputies remained sceptical, however.

"Beyond mere expressions of protocol, the president and the foreign minister should explain why precisely McCaffrey came," opposition congressman Cuauhtemoc Sandoval, secretary of the Foreign Relations Committee, told Reuters. He noted that Gurria never mentioned the planned visit during Tuesday's meeting.

On Capitol Hill, U.S. Congressmen from both the Democrat and Republican parties have sought to overturn Clinton's certification of Mexico, though they are facing an uphill battle to do so because such a resolution would need a two thirds majority in both the Senate and the House.

In the aftermath of certification, Mexico's reputation was further tarnished last week, when it announced that Humberto Garcia Abrego, brother of jailed Gulf Cartel kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego, had mysteriously given police the slip during an interrogation in police headquarters in Mexico City.
